lessons.title: What is different
lessons.objective: You can list the biggest rule differences between college and the NFL.

payload.prompt: Match each college rule to what it means.

pairs.definition: A college receiver needs only one foot inbounds; the NFL needs two.
Snapped from the 3-yard line in college, the 2 in the NFL.
Each team starts at the opponent's 25; later rounds become alternating two-point tries.
Forcible contact to the head or neck of a defenseless player: penalty and ejection.

explanation.summary: One foot, the 3-yard two-point try, a possession-based overtime and ejection for targeting are the headline differences. The plays and positions are the same.
explanation.sayThisLine: One foot is enough in college.

payload.prompt: A receiver gets one foot down and catches the ball before stepping out. That is a catch in college. True or false?

scene.alt: A receiver making a one-foot catch against the sideline in college.

explanation.correct: True. College only needs one foot. The NFL requires two feet or another body part in bounds.
explanation.incorrect: Yes, one foot is enough in college. That is the biggest receiver rule difference.

payload.prompt: Which clock fact is true in both college and the NFL?

options.text: An incomplete pass stops the clock until the next snap
An incomplete pass lets the clock keep running
The clock never stops in the last two minutes

explanation.correct: Incomplete passes stop the clock at every level, which is why passing teams save time. College and NFL clock rules differ in smaller details, like some first-down and late-game situations, so check before you claim a difference.
explanation.incorrect: An incomplete pass stops the clock in both games. The differences are in finer details, not that big a split.

statement.speaker: Analyst
statement.text: Third overtime. No more drives, just alternating two-point tries from the 3.

payload.question: What is the analyst saying?

options.text: Overtime lasts three rounds no matter what
From the third overtime, each team just gets alternating two-point tries
Teams can score safeties in overtime
Overtime only happens once per game

payload.translation: College overtime starts with each team getting the ball at the opponent's 25. After two rounds still tied, teams stop running drives and alternate two-point tries from the 3-yard line until someone leads after a full round.

followUps.line: Is that the same as NFL overtime?
followUps.why: No. The NFL plays a timed period with regular possessions. College uses a possession-based format that shifts to two-point tries later.

followUps.line: Why do people love college overtime?
followUps.why: Every possession is high stakes, and the later rounds are pure pressure.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If unsure, say it gets down to two-point tries in the third overtime and ask what they think of the format.

payload.prompt: From the third overtime on, teams alternate two-point tries instead of drives. True or false?

scene.alt: Two teams alternating short two-point tries from the 3-yard line.

explanation.correct: True. After two full rounds, college overtime shifts to alternating two-point tries from the 3-yard line.
explanation.incorrect: Yes. The drives stop and the two-point tries start once it is the third overtime.

lessons.title: Polls and the committee
lessons.objective: You can explain how college rankings and the playoff committee decide the top teams.

payload.prompt: Which ranking decides the College Football Playoff field?

options.text: The AP poll, which has been around since 1936
The Coaches poll, in which coaches vote on quality
The CFP committee rankings, released weekly starting in November

explanation.correct: The CFP committee picks and seeds the field. Its rankings start coming out in November and update weekly. The AP and Coaches polls still drive talk but do not pick the field.
explanation.incorrect: The committee rankings decide the 12-team field. They start in early November and update weekly.

payload.prompt: Put the CFP selection steps in order.

items.text: Conference champions are decided in championship weekend
The committee publishes its final ranking
The automatic-bid champions plus at-large teams fill the twelve spots
Seeds 1 to 12 are set by ranking; the top four get byes

explanation.correct: Champions are crowned, then the committee ranks, then the field is set: five automatic bids plus seven at-large teams, seeded by ranking. The top four seeds get byes.
explanation.incorrect: Champions are crowned first, then the final ranking, then the field, then seeding and byes.

payload.prompt: Match each ranking system to its role.

pairs.definition: Media voter rankings; affects perception but does not seed the playoff.
Rankings by head coaches; historic but less official now.
Official ranker for playoff selection; their Tuesday rankings matter most.

explanation.summary: Three ranking systems exist: media votes, coach votes, and the official committee. Only the committee decides the playoff.
explanation.sayThisLine: AP is media. Coaches is coaches. CFP committee is the one that matters.

statement.speaker: Fan
statement.text: We are number five in the AP poll but the committee has us at two. That is what matters.

payload.question: What is the fan saying?

options.text: The AP poll and CFP committee always agree
The committee might rank them higher than the media does, which matters more for the playoff
The media polls determine who gets into the playoff
Rankings never change after November

payload.translation: The fan is saying the committee, which picks the playoff field, ranks their team higher than the media poll does, so they feel better about their chances.

followUps.line: Why would the committee and the AP poll differ?
followUps.why: They use different voters and criteria, and the committee looks at schedule strength and results.

followUps.line: Which ranking picks the playoff field?
followUps.why: The committee. The AP poll is influential but does not decide.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If unsure, remember that the committee is the official selector; media rankings are influential but not binding.

payload.prompt: The ACC, Big 12, Big Ten and SEC champions get automatic CFP bids. True or false?

scene.alt: A conference champion celebrating a playoff berth.

explanation.correct: True for the 2026-27 format: those four champions plus the highest-ranked Group of 6 champion get automatic bids. The other seven spots are at-large.
explanation.incorrect: Yes, four conference champions plus the top Group of 6 champion are automatic. The format gets re-checked each season.

lessons.title: The 12-team playoff
lessons.objective: You can explain how the playoff bracket works, who gets byes and what a first-round win means.

payload.prompt: Put the playoff rounds in order.

items.text: First round: Seeds five through twelve play; seeds one through four get byes and play the winners
Quarterfinals: Eight teams (the bye teams plus four first-round winners) play in four games
Semifinals: The four winners play in two games, often in bowl stadiums
National championship: The two survivors play for the title

explanation.correct: Twelve teams, four bye to the quarterfinals, eight play first, then down to four, then two, then one champion.
explanation.incorrect: The playoff format proceeds from first round through quarterfinals, semifinals, and then the national championship.

payload.prompt: Why is a number-one seed so valuable in the college playoff?

options.text: They play fewer games in the early rounds because they get a bye to the quarterfinals
They always face a weaker team in the semifinals
They get home games in the first round

explanation.correct: Seeds one through four skip the first round. They play fewer games and arrive rested. The first-round games are hosted on campus by seeds five through eight.
explanation.incorrect: The bye is the advantage. Seeds one through four skip the first round, which is played at campus sites.

payload.prompt: You back the eight seed. What is your path to the quarterfinals?

facts.label: First round
facts.value: Play the nine seed on campus

facts.label: If you win
facts.value: Face the one seed in a bowl

facts.label: Rest gap
facts.value: The one seed had a bye

options.label: Beat nine, then take on a rested one seed
options.consequence: You host the nine seed in round one. If you win, you face the top seed, who is rested. That is the eight-seed story: a real shot, but a tough path.
considerations: The eight-nine game is close to a coin flip.
The one seed has a rest edge.

options.label: Assume a deep run is guaranteed
options.consequence: Nothing is guaranteed. Even the first game is competitive and the next opponent is the top seed.
considerations: Making the field is one thing; winning four games is another.

payload.expertNote: The eight seed is in the field on merit and gets a home game. The price is an extra game and a rested top seed next.

payload.prompt: Match each playoff round to what it is called and who plays.

pairs.definition: Seeds five through twelve play at campus sites; seeds one through four rest.
The four bye teams play the four first-round winners in major bowl games.
The four quarterfinal winners play in two games at bowl sites.

explanation.summary: First round is five through twelve on campus. Quarterfinals bring the bye teams in, semifinals take the four survivors, then the title game.
explanation.sayThisLine: Five through twelve first, then the bye teams join.

statement.speaker: Coach
statement.text: We have to finish in the top four or we play an extra game. Four games to a title instead of three is a big difference.

payload.question: What is the coach saying?

options.text: All twelve teams play the same number of games
Getting a bye and resting is a major advantage in the playoffs
Winning a first-round game guarantees a bye
The playoff is best of seven games

payload.translation: A bye means skipping the first round. A team with a bye needs three wins for the title, while a team that plays in round one needs four.

followUps.line: How much does a bye help?
followUps.why: Rest and prep time help, and one fewer win is needed, but teams still have to win the games.

followUps.line: Is a seed-four bye worth chasing?
followUps.why: Yes, it saves a game, though the quarterfinal opponent can still be tough.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If unsure, think about the value of a week off in sports. Every team wants extra rest.

lessons.title: Conference chaos
lessons.objective: You can explain why colleges move conferences and what realignment means to rivalries.

payload.prompt: Why do colleges leave conferences?

options.text: More television money, better playoff odds, and wanting to join stronger leagues
The coaching staff asked for it
The current conference was too old

explanation.correct: Money and prestige drive realignment. The SEC and Big Ten offer bigger TV deals and better playoff seeding. Schools chase that.
explanation.incorrect: Realignment is economics: TV deals, playoff positioning, and brand. It is not about nostalgia or tradition.

statement.speaker: Longtime Fan
statement.text: Our rival just moved to the Big Ten. We might never play them again. This realignment stuff is destroying college football.

payload.question: What is the fan saying?

options.text: Conference realignment has ended century-old rivalries because schools left for money
The Big Ten is a bad conference
Rivalries will definitely never happen again
Schools should not be allowed to move

payload.translation: The fan is upset that his school's traditional rival left for another conference, likely ending the annual game that had been played for decades. Realignment has broken many historic rivalries.

followUps.why: Sometimes, as non-conference games, but they are harder to schedule.

followUps.line: Is this good or bad for college football?
followUps.why: It is debated. Fans miss traditions; schools get more money and access.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If unsure, think about what realignment means: schools splitting apart, traditional rivals separated, new conferences formed.

payload.prompt: Match each realignment effect to what it means.

pairs.definition: Rivals move conferences and no longer play. Fans lose traditions.
Better TV deals give schools more money for athletics.
Strong conferences improve playoff odds and prestige.

explanation.summary: Realignment chases money and power. Rivalries suffer; revenue grows; strong conferences get stronger.
explanation.sayThisLine: Rivalries die, money rises, power consolidates. That is realignment.

payload.prompt: Bigger TV money and better playoff access are major reasons schools switch conferences. True or false?

scene.alt: A big stadium crowd at a rivalry game, with a conference logo.

explanation.correct: True. Media-rights money, playoff positioning and brand drive realignment.
explanation.incorrect: Tradition matters to fans, but money and access are the big drivers.

payload.prompt: Your school is offered $30M a year more to switch conferences. Your rivalry game is at risk. Worth it?

facts.label: Stakeholders
facts.value: Players, coaches, and fans all have opinions

options.label: Take the money and try to keep the rival on the schedule
options.consequence: You capture the money and work to keep the rivalry alive as a non-conference game.
considerations: $30M funds scholarships and facilities.
Keeping the game takes effort and agreement.

options.label: Take the money and let the rivalry go
options.consequence: Many schools have chosen this. The revenue is real, and fans may lose a tradition.
considerations: Budgets are real.
Fans often feel the loss.

options.label: Stay put for tradition
options.consequence: You keep the game and the identity, but fall behind financially.
considerations: Tradition matters to fans.
Revenue gaps are hard to close.

payload.expertNote: Money drives realignment, but smart schools try to protect the games that matter to fans.

lessons.title: Portal and NIL
lessons.objective: You can explain why college rosters turn over completely every year.

payload.prompt: You were benched for a veteran. The transfer portal window opens. Stay or leave?

facts.label: Portal
facts.value: A window opens after the season

facts.label: New school
facts.value: Likely eligible to play right away

options.label: Enter the portal
options.consequence: With immediate eligibility at a new school, many players in your position leave for a better shot at playing time.
considerations: Players now have real power to move.
Immediate eligibility removes the old sit-out penalty.

options.label: Stay and compete
options.consequence: Possible if the veteran is leaving soon. You keep your team and scholarship, but you risk sitting another year.
considerations: Patience can pay off.
Playing time elsewhere is tempting.

payload.expertNote: The transfer portal changed college football. Players can enter during set windows and usually play right away, so rosters turn over every year.

statement.speaker: Coach
statement.text: Half my roster is new guys from the portal. We have to rebuild team chemistry every single year now.

payload.question: What is the coach saying?

options.text: The transfer portal makes it easy to draft college players now
College rosters change drastically every year because players transfer freely, and team chemistry suffers
The coach is not doing a good job recruiting
College players stay with their teams for four years like they used to

payload.translation: The coach is frustrated that half his team is new portal transfers. Building chemistry is harder now that players can move between seasons.

followUps.line: Why would a top recruit leave after signing?
followUps.why: Tests understanding: better offer elsewhere, portal opportunity, promise broken, or lack of playing time.

followUps.line: Is the transfer portal good or bad for college football?
followUps.why: Opinion. Players like the freedom; coaches hate the instability; fans miss roster continuity.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If unsure, think: in the old days, players stayed four years. Now they leave after one bad season. That is the portal.

payload.prompt: Match each new money system to what it does.

pairs.definition: Lets players transfer, usually with no sit-out year.
Players earn from endorsements and sponsors, not just scholarships.
Since 2025-26, schools can pay athletes directly under a legal settlement.

explanation.summary: Portal lets players move. NIL lets them earn from their name. Revenue sharing adds direct payment from schools. Together they reshaped college recruiting.
explanation.sayThisLine: Free to move, paid for your name, and a share of the revenue.

payload.prompt: A college player can now usually transfer and play right away. True or false?

scene.alt: A transfer player joining a new team.

explanation.correct: True. Under the current rules, players can generally transfer and be eligible immediately, which is why rosters churn.
explanation.incorrect: Yes, the old sit-out penalty mostly went away.

payload.prompt: Which change has most disrupted college football recruiting?

options.text: The transfer portal and NIL letting players leave and earn money from their name immediately
Coaches being paid less money
The NFL draft happening earlier in the year

explanation.correct: Portal plus NIL is the earthquake. Players can move during windows, earn from their name and usually play right away.
explanation.incorrect: The portal and NIL together gave players power they never had before.

lessons.title: Recruiting
lessons.objective: You can decode recruiting talk and understand why college recruiting never stops.

payload.prompt: Match each recruiting term to what it means.

pairs.definition: A top-rated high school player, per recruiting services.
All prospects signed by a team in a year, ranked together.
When recruits sign to join a college team.

explanation.summary: Stars are ratings, classes are ranked groups and signing day is the spectacle.
explanation.sayThisLine: Five stars are top-rated, classes are groups, signing day is the show.

statement.speaker: Fan
statement.text: Our recruiting class is ranked number twelve nationally. Half of them will probably transfer out by spring.

payload.question: What is the fan saying?

options.text: The recruiting class is elite and no one will leave
A top-twelve class is good but many recruits might leave via the portal if they do not play or fit the system
Recruiting class rankings never matter
No one leaves college once they sign

payload.translation: The fan is being realistic. Even highly recruited players transfer quickly if they are unhappy, benched or want to play immediately. A good ranking does not guarantee retention.

followUps.line: Why would a top recruit leave after signing?
followUps.why: Tests understanding: better offer elsewhere, portal opportunity, promise broken, or lack of playing time.

followUps.line: Is recruiting still important if everyone transfers?
followUps.why: Yes, but less. Strong recruiting is necessary but no longer sufficient to win.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If unsure, think: a five-star has options. If unhappy, he uses the portal to leave.

payload.prompt: A team with five-star recruits will definitely win more games than a team with three-star recruits. True or false?

scene.alt: A high school star being recruited by multiple colleges.

explanation.correct: False. Star ratings are predictions, not guarantees. Coaching, development and fit matter. Many five-stars do not pan out; some lower-stars overachieve.
explanation.incorrect: Recruiting rankings are useful but imperfect. A three-star program with great coaching can beat a five-star program with poor development.

payload.prompt: How has the transfer portal changed recruiting?

options.text: Recruiting high school talent is now only half the battle; portal recruiting for transfers is equally important
Recruiting high school players is more important than ever
Recruiting does not happen anymore

explanation.correct: Strong programs now do both: recruit high school stars and poach portal players from other teams. Transfers fill gaps and provide immediate contributors.
explanation.incorrect: High school recruiting matters but so does the portal now. Top programs win the portal wars as much as the high school game.

payload.prompt: You are a five-star quarterback. Multiple schools want you. What matters most?

facts.label: Your choice
facts.value: Elite A or rising school B

facts.label: School A
facts.value: Storied, huge facilities, benched behind senior

options.label: Go to School B for immediate playing time
options.consequence: Playing time matters a lot for development and NFL exposure, and School B also offers NIL money. Many top recruits weigh this heavily.
considerations: Playing time is valuable currency.
Sitting behind a senior could cost you a year.

options.label: Go to School A for the prestigious name
options.consequence: School A's brand and NFL pipeline are real advantages, but you may sit or end up in the portal.
considerations: Prestige matters.
Playing time matters more to many players.

payload.expertNote: Modern recruiting weighs playing time, portal flexibility and NIL. Storied names still matter, but they are no longer automatic.

lessons.title: Heisman and awards
lessons.objective: You can say what a Heisman campaign is and why it matters to recruiting and draft stock.

payload.prompt: What is the Heisman Trophy?

options.text: The annual award for the most outstanding college player, voted by media, past winners and fans
The trophy given to the national champion
An award only for running backs

explanation.correct: The Heisman is an individual award for the best college player in any position. Media members and past winners vote, and fans get one collective vote.
explanation.incorrect: Heisman is the Oscars of college football: one player, any position, voted on in December.

statement.speaker: Analyst
statement.text: His Heisman campaign is in full swing. Every media story, every highlight reel, every stat is designed to remind voters he belongs.

payload.question: What is the analyst describing?

options.text: The player is running for political office
The orchestrated effort to get a player's name in front of voters for the Heisman award
The player is injured and cannot play
The team is losing games

payload.translation: A Heisman campaign is the strategic push to get a player in the award conversation. Teams, media, and even players push stats and highlights to voters all season.

followUps.why: Media members, past winners and one fan vote. Campaigns aim at the media voters.

followUps.line: Can a player on a bad team win?
followUps.why: Rarely. Winning teams and big moments help a lot.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If unsure, think about the Oscars: campaigning, highlighting performances, and voting. The Heisman is very similar.

payload.prompt: Match each college football award to what it honors.

pairs.definition: Most outstanding player in college football.
Title for the CFP playoff winner.
Elite players at each position; stepping stone to NFL.

explanation.summary: Heisman is one player. National title is the team. All-America is the all-star team. Each matters for different reasons.
explanation.sayThisLine: Heisman is the best player. Championship is the best team. All-America is the elite squad.

payload.prompt: A Heisman winner is guaranteed a top-ten NFL draft pick. True or false?

scene.alt: A Heisman trophy beside a draft board.

explanation.correct: False. Many winners go high, but some, such as Johnny Manziel at 22nd, went outside the top ten.
explanation.incorrect: The Heisman is a strong signal, not a guarantee.

payload.prompt: You are a star running back on a losing team. Can you win the Heisman?

facts.label: Heisman voters
facts.value: Often favor players on winning teams

options.label: Very unlikely
options.consequence: Voters heavily favor stars on winning teams. Elite stats alone usually are not enough.
considerations: A losing record hurts a Heisman case.

options.label: You are a lock
options.consequence: Not true. Voters weigh team success and national attention heavily.
considerations: Context matters hugely for the Heisman.

payload.expertNote: Heisman voters reward stars on winning teams. A losing record hurts even great stats.

lessons.title: Rivalry week
lessons.objective: You can talk about rivalry games without insulting anyone and understand why they matter.

statement.speaker: Longtime Fan
statement.text: In a rivalry game, records do not matter. Everything we learned during the season gets thrown out. It is pure passion and tradition.

payload.question: What is the fan saying?

options.text: Rivalry games are just normal games with a lot of emotion
Rivalry games transcend records and stats; tradition and pride override normal game logic
Rivalry games are played in a different season
Rivalries have no impact on the playoff picture

payload.translation: The fan means the standings matter less in this game. Fans say a 3-9 team can beat a 12-0 team because the history and pride are so strong.

followUps.line: Do rivalry games really go by form?
followUps.why: Not always. Upsets happen often enough to feed the legend, though the better team still wins more often.

followUps.line: Why do rivalries matter if they are just games?
followUps.why: They are cultural events. A loss stings until next year.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If unsure, think about why fans care so much about rivalry games beyond just winning or losing.

payload.prompt: Match each rivalry element to what it represents.

pairs.definition: A game played for generations, like Ohio State-Michigan, first played in 1897.
An annual game where fans say the records get thrown out.
A pre-game party where fans gather. Part of the tradition.

explanation.summary: Rivalries are traditions first, games second. Every rivalry has a history, a yearly matchup, and a unique culture.
explanation.sayThisLine: History is the tradition, the game is the event, the tailgate is the culture.

payload.title: Talking about a big rivalry game
payload.setting: During rivalry week, when emotions are high.

exchanges.theirMessage: I cannot wait for the rivalry game next week. We always lose to them, but this year feels different.

replies.text: Why does this year feel different? What have you seen?
replies.theirResponse: Our quarterback has been amazing this season and their defense is banged up.
replies.coachNote: Shows you care about their reasoning, not just emotion.

replies.theirResponse: They are. I hope we finally beat them.
replies.coachNote: True, but vague. Dig into their specific prediction.

replies.text: You always say that and you always lose.
replies.coachNote: Do not laugh at their hope. They are sharing something they care about.

payload.prompt: What happens to a team after losing a big rivalry game?

options.text: The loss stings more than a regular loss and fans stay upset for weeks
It is the same as any other loss
The team is eliminated from the playoffs

explanation.correct: A rivalry loss stings more than an ordinary one, and the next meeting becomes bigger for it.
explanation.incorrect: Rivalry losses carry cultural weight that lasts until the next meeting.

payload.prompt: Your team is 3-9 and the rival is 9-3, heading into their matchup. What is the likely outcome?

facts.label: Stakes
facts.value: Bragging rights and rival team's playoff fate

options.label: Your team has a real shot to upset them
options.consequence: In a rivalry, a 3-9 team can beat a 9-3 team. Pride and nothing to lose are powerful, even if the better team is still favored.
considerations: Rivalries feed the upset legend.
The better team still wins more often.

options.label: The 9-3 team is guaranteed to win
options.consequence: No guarantee in a rivalry. Your team may play loose because it has nothing to lose.
considerations: Desperation plus tradition is dangerous.

payload.expertNote: Rivalry upsets are famous because they feel like they happen often. The better team is still favored, but not safe.
